key_terms.meaning: The whole set of units about which a conclusion is wanted, described by fixed unknown parameters such as μ and σ².
A subset of n units drawn from the population; the data actually observed.
A fixed but unknown number describing the population, written with Greek letters: μ, σ², p.
Any function of the sample values alone, carrying no unknown parameter, such as x̄ or S².
The probability distribution of a statistic over all possible samples of size n; it has a mean and a variance of its own.
Each draw is independent and every unit has probability 1/N at every draw, so P(sample) = (1/N)ⁿ.
The gap between a statistic and the parameter caused purely by which units happened to be drawn; it shrinks as n grows.
Error from sources other than sampling — wrong entries, faulty instruments, non-response; it does not vanish by increasing n.
The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a statistic; for the mean it is SE(x̄) = σ/√n.

key_terms.term: Standard error of the sample proportion
key_terms.meaning: SE(p̂) = √(p(1−p)/n), where p̂ = X/n and X is the count of successes.
If Z₁,…,Z_k are independent standard normal, then ΣZᵢ² ~ χ²(k), with mean k and variance 2k; here k is the degrees of freedom.
T = Z/√(V/k) where Z ~ N(0,1), V ~ χ²(k), Z and V independent; symmetric, heavier tails than normal, tends to N(0,1) as k → ∞.
F = (U/k₁)/(V/k₂) where U ~ χ²(k₁), V ~ χ²(k₂) are independent; used for ratios of two sample variances.
The number of independent pieces of information left in a sum of squares; n−1 for S² computed from n observations.
An estimator T of θ with E(T) = θ for every θ; its errors cancel on average over repeated samples.
Tₙ is consistent for θ if Tₙ → θ in probability as n → ∞; enough that bias → 0 and variance → 0.
MSE(T) = E[(T − θ)²] = Var(T) + [bias(T)]², the average squared distance from the parameter.
The value θ̂ that maximises the likelihood L(θ) = Π f(xᵢ; θ), i.e. makes the observed sample most probable.
ℓ(θ) = log L(θ); maximised at the same point as L, and easier to differentiate for products.
A random interval [L, U] built from the sample with P(L ≤ θ ≤ U) = 1 − α; here 1 − α is the confidence level.
A function of the data and the parameter whose distribution does not depend on any unknown parameter, used to build intervals.
For independent observations with mean μ and finite variance σ², (x̄ − μ)/(σ/√n) → N(0,1) in distribution as n → ∞.

takeaways: A statistic is a random variable, so it has a distribution; estimation is the study of that distribution.
With replacement sampling, E(x̄) = μ and Var(x̄) = σ²/n, so the standard error falls only as fast as 1/√n.
The central limit theorem makes x̄ approximately normal for large n even when the population is not normal.
S² is unbiased for σ², and (n−1)S²/σ² has a chi-square distribution when the population is normal.
The t distribution replaces σ by S and adds the extra uncertainty of a small sample.
MSE = variance + bias², so a slightly biased estimator with much smaller variance can be the better choice.
The maximum likelihood method turns a product of densities into a sum of logs and usually gives a consistent, efficient estimator.
A 95% confidence interval is a procedure that covers the parameter in 95% of repeated samples, not a 95% chance for this one interval.
Chi-square, t and F are all built from normal samples: squares, ratios, and ratios of averages of squares.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask you to derive a sampling distribution from scratch, state the assumptions, and then use it for an interval or a test, so keep the derivation and the numerical application in one flow.

bank.q: Define population, sample, parameter and statistic. Distinguish sampling error from non-sampling error, and derive the mean and variance of the sample mean under simple random sampling with replacement.
outline: Parameter is fixed and unknown; statistic is a function of the sample and is a random variable.
With replacement, draws are independent and each has distribution of X.
E(x̄) = (1/n)ΣE(Xᵢ) = μ; Var(x̄) = (1/n²)ΣVar(Xᵢ) = σ²/n.
Standard error is σ/√n; it measures sampling error, which falls with n.
Non-sampling error comes from measurement and recording and does not fall with n.

bank.q: State the central limit theorem and explain how it is used to approximate the distribution of the sample mean and of a sample proportion.
outline: Statement for i.i.d. variables with mean μ and finite variance σ².
Standardisation (x̄ − μ)/(σ/√n) → N(0,1).
Remark that no assumption on the shape of the population is needed.
Proportion case: p̂ has mean p and variance p(1−p)/n, approximately normal for large n.
Continuity correction and the usual rule of thumb for n.

bank.q: Define the chi-square, t and F distributions, give the sampling situations in which each arises from normal samples, and state one use of each.
outline: Chi-square as a sum of squares of independent standard normals; mean k, variance 2k.
t as a normal divided by the root of an independent chi-square over its degrees of freedom.
F as a ratio of two independent chi-square variables each divided by its degrees of freedom.
Occurrence: (n−1)S²/σ² is chi-square; (x̄ − μ)/(S/√n) is t; S₁²/S₂² scaled is F.
Uses: variance intervals, small-sample mean tests, equality of two variances.

bank.q: Define unbiasedness, efficiency, consistency and mean squared error for a point estimator, and prove MSE = variance + bias².
outline: E(T) = θ for unbiasedness; bias b(θ) = E(T) − θ.
Efficiency as smaller variance among unbiased estimators.
Consistency as convergence in probability, guaranteed by bias → 0 and variance → 0.
Expansion of E[(T − θ)²] about E(T) gives Var(T) + b².
Example showing a biased estimator with smaller MSE can be preferred.

bank.q: Derive the maximum likelihood estimator of p for a Bernoulli sample, and of λ for a Poisson sample. Check that each is unbiased and consistent.
outline: Likelihood for Bernoulli: p^Σx (1−p)^(n−Σx).
Log-likelihood differentiation gives p̂ = x̄.
Poisson: ℓ = −nλ + Σx log λ, giving λ̂ = x̄.
E(p̂) = p and Var(p̂) = p(1−p)/n, so unbiased and consistent.
Same for λ̂: mean λ, variance λ/n, consistency follows.

bank.q: Derive a 100(1 − α)% confidence interval for the mean of a normal population when σ is known, and explain carefully what the confidence level means.
outline: Choose z_{α/2} with P(−z ≤ Z ≤ z) = 1 − α.
Invert to get x̄ ± z_{α/2} σ/√n.
The interval is random; 1 − α is the long-run coverage over repeated samples.
Numerical example with n, x̄, σ and α.

bank.q: A random sample of 16 items from a normal population gives x̄ = 42.5 and s = 4.0. Construct a 95% confidence interval for μ without assuming σ is known, and explain why the t distribution is used.
outline: σ unknown, so use the pivot (x̄ − μ)/(S/√n) ~ t(15).
t value with 15 degrees of freedom at 2.5% tail.
State the assumption of normality and independent observations.
Interpretation as coverage, not as probability for this fixed μ.

bank.q: Derive a 100(1 − α)% confidence interval for the variance σ² of a normal population using the chi-square distribution, and for the ratio of two variances using the F distribution.
outline: Pivot (n−1)S²/σ² ~ χ²(n−1).
Choose two chi-square quantiles to split α equally.
Invert to get the interval for σ²; take square roots for σ.
F case: pivot (S₁²/σ₁²)/(S₂²/σ₂²) ~ F(n₁−1, n₂−1).
Intervals are not symmetric, and the F limits are reciprocals of each other.

bank.q: Show that the sample variance S² = Σ(Xᵢ − x̄)²/(n−1) is unbiased for σ², and that (n−1)S²/σ² has a chi-square distribution with n−1 degrees of freedom when the population is normal.
outline: Write Σ(Xᵢ − x̄)² = Σ(Xᵢ − μ)² − n(x̄ − μ)².
Take expectations using E[(Xᵢ − μ)²] = σ² and Var(x̄) = σ²/n.
Result E(S²) = σ²; the divisor n−1 corrects the downward bias.
For normality, (Xᵢ − μ)/σ are independent standard normals and the sum of squares splits into a chi-square plus the independent mean term.
Independence of x̄ and S² in normal samples is the key step.

bank.q: Compare the method of moments and the method of maximum likelihood. Illustrate with the normal distribution and state the invariance property of maximum likelihood estimates.
outline: Method of moments equates sample moments to population moments.
MLE maximises the likelihood; for normal it gives μ̂ = x̄ and σ̂² = Σ(Xᵢ − x̄)²/n.
The MLE of σ² is biased but consistent; the moment estimator coincides here.
Invariance: if θ̂ maximises L, then g(θ̂) maximises the likelihood of g(θ).
Trade-off: MLE needs a distributional assumption but is usually efficient.

bank.q: A 95% confidence interval computed from one sample is [3.2, 4.8]. Explain why it is wrong to say the parameter lies in this interval with probability 0.95, and evaluate the effect of sample size and confidence level on the width.
outline: Parameter is a fixed number; the endpoints are random.
Coverage probability belongs to the procedure, not to the computed interval.
Width falls as 1/√n; quadrupling n halves the width.
Raising confidence level widens the interval.
Trade-off between precision and confidence; also mention the role of assumptions.

bank.q: For a random sample from N(μ, σ²) with σ unknown, derive the sampling distribution of x̄ and of (x̄ − μ)/(S/√n), and use the result to obtain both an interval estimate and a test for μ.
outline: x̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n); standardisation gives a standard normal.
(n−1)S²/σ² ~ χ²(n−1) and is independent of x̄.
Ratio of a standard normal to the root of an independent chi-square over its degrees of freedom is t(n−1).
Interval x̄ ± t_{α/2} S/√n.
Test statistic t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(S/√n) with n−1 degrees of freedom; reject for large |t|.

bank.q: Two estimators of a parameter are available: one unbiased with large variance, one slightly biased with small variance. Explain how mean squared error settles the choice, and relate the argument to consistency.
outline: MSE = Var + bias²; compare the two numbers, not the bias alone.
Give a numerical comparison to show the biased one can win.
Consistency needs both bias and variance to vanish as n → ∞, so both estimators can be consistent.
Finite-sample choice may differ from large-sample choice.
Mention that bias can sometimes be traded deliberately, as with n−1 versus n divisors.

bank.q: Obtain the maximum likelihood estimators of μ and σ² for a normal sample, and hence construct the large-sample confidence interval for μ that uses the estimated variance.
outline: Log-likelihood −(n/2)log(2πσ²) − Σ(xᵢ − μ)²/(2σ²).
Differentiate in μ and σ² to get μ̂ = x̄ and σ̂² = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)²/n.
Second derivative or information check for a maximum.
Substitute σ̂ in the pivot and use the normal approximation for large n.
Note the difference between σ̂² and the unbiased S².

glossary.def: A statistic used to guess an unknown parameter; it is a random variable before the data are seen.
The numerical value the estimator takes on one particular sample.
b(θ) = E(T) − θ, the average signed error of an estimator over repeated samples.
Of two unbiased estimators, the one with the smaller variance is more efficient.
A statistic that captures all the information in the sample about the parameter.
L(θ) = Π f(xᵢ; θ) read as a function of θ with the data held fixed.
The derivative of the log-likelihood with respect to the parameter; it is zero at the maximum likelihood estimate.
If θ̂ is the maximum likelihood estimate of θ, then g(θ̂) is the maximum likelihood estimate of g(θ).
The long-run proportion 1 − α of samples whose interval covers the true parameter.
P(L ≤ θ ≤ U) computed over the sampling distribution of the interval endpoints.
The quantile of a reference distribution beyond which the chosen tail probability α lies.
The number of independent squared deviations entering a statistic; n−1 for a single sample variance.
A test comparing observed counts with expected counts, statistic Σ(O − E)²/E, using a chi-square reference distribution.
Z = (X − μ)/σ, with mean 0 and variance 1.
The list of units from which the sample is actually drawn.
p̂ = X/n, the fraction of successes in n independent trials, with mean p and variance p(1−p)/n.
A weighted average of two sample variances used when two populations are assumed to have equal variance.
A rule giving a lower and upper limit from the sample, together with a confidence level.
A quantity combining data and parameter whose distribution is free of unknown parameters.
The property that a standardised estimator approaches a normal distribution as n grows.
σ/√n when σ is known; S/√n when it is estimated from the sample.
σ² = E[(X − μ)²], a fixed unknown parameter of the population distribution.
Independent observations, each having the same distribution as the population.
The area beyond a critical value in one or both tails of a distribution.
